analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and other care employers to put workplace violence prevention plans in place.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 254-166 in April 2021 with every voting Democrat and 38 Republicans in favor, but the Senate committee never took it up and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Health care and social service workers face some of the highest rates of on-the-job assault of any occupation — from patients, clients, and visitors. This bill would have directed the Department of Labor to write a federal workplace violence prevention standard requiring covered employers — hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, home health agencies, emergency responders, and similar settings — to develop written violence prevention plans with employee input, assess hazards, install protections like alarms and access controls, investigate every incident, keep a violent-incident log for five years, train staff annually, and report data to the government. It also would have tied compliance to Medicare participation for hospitals and nursing homes not otherwise covered by workplace safety law. The House passed it 254-166 on April 16, 2021; the Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of nurses, aides, technicians, EMTs and paramedics, social workers, and home health and hospice workers in hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, group homes, and field settings. The bill gave them a legally enforceable right to a workplace violence prevention plan, annual training, incident investigations with employee participation, protection from retaliation for reporting violence, and access to the employer's incident records. Patients and the public benefit indirectly: staffing teams, flagging systems for clients with violence histories, and emergency response procedures make care settings safer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care and social service workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Labor Department to issue a violence prevention standard within one year, based on OSHA's own 2015 guidelines, requiring covered employers to build and maintain a written workplace violence prevention plan for each facility and service [S4][S5].

Plans must be developed with the participation of direct-care employees and their representatives, include patient-specific and environmental risk assessments, hazard corrections (alarms, access controls, barrier protection, staffing teams), reporting procedures, and anti-retaliation policies [S5].

Employers must investigate every violent incident, keep a five-year violent incident log, provide annual in-person training in a language and vocabulary workers understand, and let employees examine the records [S5].
Hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not otherwise covered by federal workplace safety law would have to comply with the standard as a condition of participating in Medicare [S5].
The bill expressly preserves workers' rights to report violence to law enforcement and adds protections on top of any state law or union contract [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric and substance-use treatment facilities, home health agencies, ambulance and emergency services, and staffing firms — all of whom would bear the cost of written plans, annual training, security equipment, incident investigation, and five years of recordkeeping. The Department of Labor would bear the cost of writing the standard and collecting annual reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and care providers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed significant compliance costs on health care employers, many already operating on thin margins, and required security staffing, training, and engineering controls whose costs the record does not quantify [S5].

It bypassed OSHA's usual rulemaking: the interim standard would have taken effect after only a 30-day comment period, with the normal notice-and-comment requirements, the Paperwork Reduction Act, and executive regulatory review waived [S5].

The mandate extended to home health, hospice, and emergency response field settings, where the exclusion covers only workers privately hired by a household — leaving the boundary between household employers and agencies to be worked out in enforcement [S5].

Critics in the House minority argued a one-size-fits-all federal standard was unnecessary because OSHA could already cite violence under its general duty clause; the House rejected that view but it was the core objection on the floor [S8].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and fall on a workforce that government injury data has long shown faces elevated assault risk, and the bill was built around a prevention model (employee participation, hazard correction, incident logging) that OSHA itself had already endorsed in voluntary guidelines since 2015. The costs are real but bounded: plans, training, and controls scaled to each facility, with a year of technical assistance before enforcement. The main design criticism is the fast-tracked rulemaking that skipped normal cost-benefit review — a fair point, though the bill did allow a final standard to be set no lower than the strongest state-level standard only if found feasible. On balance the protections outweigh the compliance burden for most covered employers.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 254-166 on April 16, 2021, but when the Senate received it three days later it went straight to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never held a vote, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced February 22, 2021, with 145 cosponsors (139 Democrats and 6 Republicans) [S6][S7].

The House Education and Labor Committee ordered it reported on a 27-20 vote on March 24, 2021, and it was reported amended on April 5, with the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees discharged from consideration [S7].
The House passed it 254-166 on April 16, 2021: all 216 voting Democrats in favor and 38 of 212 voting Republicans in favor [S8].

The Senate received the bill on April 19, 2021, read it twice, and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the record shows no further Senate action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital, nursing home, home health, and emergency services employers came out ahead: they avoided the compliance mandate for workplace violence plans, training, and recordkeeping. Health care and social service workers remain without a federal violence prevention standard.

for.name: Rep. Joe Courtney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee to House passage.

for.name: House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and ordered it reported amended, 27-20, on March 24, 2021.

against.name: 166 of 212 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, keeping the House total short of the Senate's practical threshold.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 19, 2021 and never reported it or scheduled action; the bill died there.

against.name: Hospital and long-term care industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a costly, inflexible mandate on hospitals and nursing homes.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party — 216 of 217 voting Democrats yes versus 38 of 212 voting Republicans yes — though 38 Republican votes made the 254-166 passage genuinely bipartisan in total; no Senate vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have required violence prevention plans, training, incident logs, and physical protections at every covered hospital, funded by the hospitals themselves. Their interest in avoiding the compliance cost ran against the workers and patients the protections would serve; compliance was also tied to Medicare participation for facilities not otherwise under OSHA coverage [S5].

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Residential care settings — nursing homes, hospices, memory care — are among the highest-risk environments and would have faced the full plan, log, and training requirements, with Medicare participation as the enforcement lever [S5].
Field services in private homes were explicitly covered; agencies would have had to extend prevention plans, coordination procedures, and training to workers alone in clients' homes [S5].
Emergency services and transport, including firefighters and emergency responders, were covered services subject to the standard [S5].

industries.industry: Health care staffing and temp agencies
industries.note: Contractors, subcontractors, temporary services, and employee leasing firms were expressly treated as covered employers, closing a common route around workplace safety obligations [S5].
